title: Episode 93: The Hindenburg Disaster at Lakehurst: 'Oh, the Humanity!'
description:
On May 6, 1937, the pride of German commercial aviation, the LZ-129 Hindenburg, burst into flames while docking at Lakehurst Naval Air Station in New Jersey. The disaster, captured in live radio and newsreel footage, brought the era of commercial airships to an abrupt and fiery end.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we visit the pine barrens of Ocean County, New Jersey, to witness one of the most iconic, shocking, and visceral tragedies of the twentieth century: the crash of the German zeppelin Hindenburg on May sixth, nineteen thirty-seven. Stretching longer than three football fields, the Hindenburg was the undisputed titan of the skies, an aerial luxury liner designed to conquer intercontinental travel with piano lounges, fine dining, and five-star luxury. But inflated with seven million cubic feet of explosive hydrogen gas, it was also a floating bomb. In just thirty-four seconds, captured live by radio reporter Herbert Morrison and newsreel cameras, the giant of the skies became an inferno, forever shattering human faith in the era of passenger airships. Here is George with the full, gripping story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE TITAN OF THE SKIES
In the spring of nineteen thirty-seven, the German zeppelin LZ-one-twenty-nine Hindenburg was the undisputed marvel of world commercial aviation. Built by the Luftschiffbau Zeppelin company in Friedrichshafen, Germany, under the leadership of veteran aeronaut Hugo Eckener, the Hindenburg was the largest aircraft ever constructed by human hands. It measured a staggering eight hundred and four feet in length—longer than three Boeing seven-forty-sevens placed nose-to-tail and only seventy feet shorter than the Titanic. With a hull diameter of one hundred and thirty-five feet, the colossal silver airship displaced over seven million cubic feet of gas, powered across the oceans by four massive Daimler-Benz sixteen-cylinder diesel engines that propelled it at cruise speeds exceeding eighty miles per hour.
Inside its lightweight duralumin girder skeleton lay passenger accommodations that rivaled the finest luxury ocean liners of Europe. Spread across two enclosed decks inside the belly of the hull were twenty-five private double-berth sleeping cabins, a lavish dining salon serving gourmet meals on fine Bavarian china, a writing room, and a passenger lounge complete with an ultra-lightweight duralumin grand piano covered in yellow pigskin. Along the outer walls, slanted observation windows provided passengers with panoramic vistas of the Atlantic ocean and passing icebergs while they strolled in comfortable, climate-controlled warmth.
Yet beneath the opulence lay a fatal, geopolitical compromise. The Hindenburg had been meticulously designed to operate with helium, an inert, non-flammable gas that would have eliminated all fire risk. But virtually the entire world's commercial supply of helium was located in natural gas fields in Texas, and under the Helium Control Act of nineteen twenty-seven, the United States Congress banned the export of the strategic gas to foreign powers, fearing Nazi military rearmament. With helium denied, German engineers were forced to redesign the ship's internal gas cells to carry seven million cubic feet of hydrogen: the lightest gas in the universe, but catastrophically flammable.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE TRANSATLANTIC VOYAGE
On the evening of Monday, May third, nineteen thirty-seven, the Hindenburg departed Frankfurt, Germany, embarking on its first scheduled transatlantic crossing of the nineteen thirty-seven passenger season. It was the airship's sixty-third flight, following a triumphant nineteen thirty-six inaugural season in which it had crossed the North and South Atlantic sixty-two times without a single mechanical mishap, transporting over three thousand passengers and becoming a flying symbol of German technological supremacy and prestige.
Aboard for the voyage were thirty-six passengers and sixty-one crew members, commanded by veteran Zeppelin Captain Max Pruss, with senior company director Captain Ernst Lehmann observing from the bridge. The passenger manifest included prominent socialites, industrialists, and German air ministry officials, who enjoyed three days of serene travel over the North Atlantic. Passengers drank Rhine wine in the dining salon, sent telegrams from three thousand feet, and smoked cigars in a specially pressurized, airtight smoking room fitted with an electric lighter, strictly guarded by a steward who confiscated all matches at the boarding ramp.
As the airship reached the coast of North America on the afternoon of May sixth, severe springtime thunderstorms swept across the Mid-Atlantic states. Arriving over New York Harbor at three o'clock, Captain Pruss was informed by the Lakehurst Naval Air Station in Ocean County, New Jersey, that high winds and lightning made docking unsafe. Pruss leisurely circled over Manhattan, giving passengers stunning views of the Empire State Building and Central Park, before cruising south along the New Jersey coast while waiting for the squall line to pass.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE APPROACH TO LAKEHURST
By six o'clock in the evening, weather conditions at Lakehurst began to improve. The base commander, veteran American naval airship officer Commander Charles Rosendahl, sent an urgent radio message to the Hindenburg informing Captain Pruss that surface winds were subsiding and advising an immediate landing before another storm front arrived. At seven o'clock, the massive silver silhouette of the Hindenburg loomed out of the overcast clouds over Lakehurst, gleaming against the wet pine barrens as it approached the colossal naval airship hangar.
On the airfield below, a civilian landing crew of over two hundred men—comprising ninety-two naval personnel and one hundred and thirty-nine commercial civilian laborers—stood ready on the wet sand. Gathered near the mooring mast were news photographers, newsreel camera crews from Pathé, Movietone, and Paramount, and twenty-eight-year-old radio reporter Herbert Morrison, who had traveled from WLS in Chicago with sound engineer Charlie Nehlsen to record an audio broadcast of the docking for later transmission.
To align the airship with the ground crew into a shifting wind, Captain Pruss executed a sharp, high-speed S-turn approach, maneuvering the massive hull toward the mooring mast at an altitude of two hundred feet. At seven twenty-one, the forward handling lines—heavy ropes dropped from the bow—cascaded down to the ground crew, who seized them to haul the ship toward the mechanical mooring car. Water ballast was dropped from the stern to trim the ship, while light drizzles continued to fall across the airfield.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THIRTY-FOUR SECONDS OF HORROR
At precisely seven twenty-five in the evening, a faint, flickering blue glow—likely St. Elmo's fire caused by static electrical discharge—was noticed dancing along the fabric near the top of the upper vertical tail fin. Seconds later, a small tongue of orange flame erupted from the fabric just forward of the fin, near gas cells four and five. Before the ground crew could process what was happening, an immense, deafening detonation ripped through the stern of the airship.
The seven million cubic feet of pure hydrogen gas ignited with terrifying speed. In a fraction of a second, an ocean of roaring flame swept through the interior duralumin framework, consuming the cotton gas cells and blowing out the fabric skin. The stern immediately lost all buoyancy and plunged toward the ground like a stone, pointing the fiery bow hundreds of feet into the sky like a colossal Roman candle. Down on the field, the mooring crew dropped the handling lines and fled in terror as superheated structural girders and burning debris rained across the sand.
Standing near the mooring mast, Herbert Morrison watched the catastrophe unfold through tears of shock, shouting into his microphone the immortal words that would echo through broadcasting history: 'It's burst into flames! Get out of the way, please, oh my, this is terrible, oh my, get out of the way, please! It's burning, bursting into flames and is falling on the mooring mast and all the folks agree this is terrible, this is one of the worst catastrophes in the world! Oh, the humanity and all the passengers screaming around here!'
From the first spark to the moment the burning skeleton collapsed into a twisted pile of white-hot duralumin on the New Jersey sand, exactly thirty-four seconds had elapsed. The titan of the skies was reduced to a smoldering, incandescent heap of ash.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MIRACULOUS SURVIVORS
Given the apocalyptic fury of the explosion and the speed with which the colossal airship was consumed by fire, the most astonishing fact of the Hindenburg disaster was that the majority of those on board survived. Of the ninety-seven passengers and crew members on the airship, sixty-two miraculously survived, while thirty-five perished in the flames, along with one member of the civilian ground crew on the airfield below, bringing the total death toll to thirty-six.
Survival was determined largely by split-second decisions and sheer geographical fortune within the ship. As the stern hit the ground, the passenger decks in the lower forward hull remained intact for several seconds before the bow crashed downward. Panic-stricken passengers and crew smashed open observation windows and leaped onto the wet sand from heights of twenty to thirty feet. Some broke bones upon impact but were dragged clear of the falling inferno by heroic ground crew members and naval sailors who ran directly into the blazing debris with coats and blankets to pull survivors from the wreckage.
Captain Max Pruss suffered severe facial burns but survived, while company director Ernst Lehmann was pulled from the burning control car with fatal burns, whispering his final words in a military hospital the following morning: 'I cannot understand it.' Heroic cabin boys, stewards, and passengers survived by diving beneath overturned water tanks or crawling through broken fuselage gaps seconds before the roof collapsed in a shower of liquid metal.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE INVESTIGATION AND THE SABOTAGE THEORIES
Immediately following the disaster, joint investigatory commissions were convened by the United States Department of Commerce and the German Air Ministry to determine the root cause of the tragedy. Because the Hindenburg was the flagship of Nazi Germany, adorned with massive swastikas across its tail fins, rampant rumors of anti-fascist sabotage and timed bombs circulated wildly in the international press. High-ranking Nazi officials, including Hermann Göring, initially suspected communist sabotage, pointing to suspicious letters received by the embassy in Washington.
However, months of exhaustive metallurgical testing, chemical analysis, and eyewitness testimony conclusively ruled out intentional sabotage. The official American investigation, led by Commander South Trimble, concluded that the disaster was caused by electrostatic discharge. As the Hindenburg executed its sharp S-turns through the damp thunderstorm atmosphere, one of the interior bracing wire cables likely snapped, whipping into gas cell number four and tearing the delicate fabric, allowing hydrogen to leak into the unventilated cavity between the gas cells and the outer hull.
When the damp landing lines touched the wet ground, the airship's metal duralumin framework was instantly grounded to the earth. However, the outer fabric skin, coated with a cellulose butyrate and iron oxide waterproofing dope, remained electrically charged by the surrounding thunderstorm atmosphere. The extreme difference in electrical potential between the grounded frame and the charged skin caused an electrostatic spark to jump across the gap, igniting the leaking hydrogen cloud in an instantaneous chain reaction.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE END OF THE AIRSHIP ERA
The destruction of the Hindenburg was not the deadliest aviation disaster in history—the crash of the American rigid airship USS Akron off the New Jersey coast in nineteen thirty-three had claimed seventy-three lives, and the British R-one-oh-one had killed forty-eight. But Johnstown and the Akron had vanished unseen into the ocean darkness. The Hindenburg was different. It was the first modern technological catastrophe captured live on audio recording and captured from multiple camera angles on motion picture newsreel.
Within hours, Herbert Morrison's gut-wrenching audio broadcast was played over nationwide radio networks, and within days, millions of moviegoers sat in darkened theaters around the globe watching the terrifying footage of the silver giant incinerating in thirty-four seconds. The psychological impact on the public imagination was instantaneous and devastating. The illusion that passenger airships represented a safe, majestic future of luxury travel was permanently extinguished in a flash of orange flame.
Within months, commercial zeppelin operations were grounded indefinitely. Hugo Eckener's newly completed sister ship, the LZ-one-thirty Graf Zeppelin II, was converted into a military radar surveillance craft before being ordered scrapped by Hermann Göring in nineteen forty, its precious duralumin melted down to build fighter aircraft for the Luftwaffe. The age of the colossal rigid airship was over, superseded by faster, safer, multi-engine fixed-wing passenger aircraft like the Douglas DC-three and Boeing three-fourteen Clipper.
Today, at Lakehurst Naval Air Station, a modest bronze plaque set into the sandy pine earth marks the exact spot where the Hindenburg's bow touched the ground. Overhead, the immense silhouette of Hangar Number One still stands sentinel against the New Jersey sky, a monumental cathedral of aviation history remembering the afternoon when the titan of the skies was swallowed by flame.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The fiery collapse of the Hindenburg at Lakehurst brought the magnificent era of giant passenger zeppelins to an abrupt, tragic close. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we step into colonial Connecticut for the legendary midnight defiance of the Charter Oak.
